members.title: `_close_recovered` can close an `unexpected_fault` escalation after one clean tick
members.description: `_close_recovered` closes every open project escalation whose `fault_kind` is not in this tick's `TickFaults.kinds()`. `unexpected_fault` is written by `escalate()` in `faults.py`. It goes straight to `store.raise_project_escalation`, never through `TickFaults`, so it is never in the recurring set. The next tick that completes without cut-off therefore closes it. That includes the case where the node had a run in flight and `escalate` deliberately took the project-scoped path instead of blocking the node. A real, intermittent planner or decide bug would open and close an escalation within seconds, and no human gets a durable signal. If that is intended, say so in the `_close_recovered` docstring. If not, close only kinds the tick can re-observe (`run_observation_failed`, `launch_overdue`, `cf_probe_failed`) and leave `unexpected_fault` for a human to close. The store docstring says the `fault_kind` vocabulary is the Runner's. That makes an explicit allowlist cheap and safe against other writers later.

members.title: `status_reads` repeats the unit/request join and breaks the manifest modules' single-home rule
members.description: `_UNITS` repeats `UNIT_FROM` from `manifest_reads.py:90`. That join is also written inline in `manifest_reads.py` at lines 167–170 and 199–201. The docstring at `manifest_reads.py:5-6` says every SQL statement on `tick_request` and `tick_archive_unit` lives in one of three modules (`manifest_reads`, `manifest_request_reads`, `manifest_repo`). `status_reads.py` is a fourth home. Fix: import `UNIT_FROM`, or move the status SQL into one of those three modules.

members.title: Over-session names are keyed by product, not family, and a missing key is silently defaulted
members.description: `_family_evidence` collects `over` names into `named[product]` across every coverage read for that product, both ES `ohlcv-1m` and ES `statistics`. `over_failures` then attaches the whole list to each family row for that product. So a bar-family failure can name statistics sessions, and the reverse. Each `volume_verdict_dict` carries a `family` field (`src/manta_trading/data/tick/tick_coverage.py:93`) that could key the list. Separately, `over_sessions` uses `coverage.get("volume_checks") or ()` (`scripts/purchase_accounting.py:112`). That default swallows an absent key, although the module docstring says every key is required and a missing one raises. The failure still fires, because the count comes from `cross_tier`, so the impact is on the names.

members.title: Over-session names are attributed to the wrong volume family
members.description: `named` is keyed by product only (scripts/cutover_304_evidence.py:216, 232-233), and `over_sessions` takes every `over` verdict regardless of family (purchase_accounting.py:105-116). The statistics coverage document carries volume checks for both volume families (`VOLUME_FAMILIES` in src/manta_trading/data/tick/schema_families.py:53-56, iterated in tick_coverage_statistics.py:61-71). Each verdict has a `family` field (tick_coverage.py:93). So `over_failures` attaches every ES over session to both the ES tick-tier row and the ES bar_1m row. The count is right, but the names can be wrong, and D6 item 4 requires naming. The test fixture for `over_sessions` omits `family`, so this is not exercised. Key the names by (product, family) and filter by family.

members.title: Over-volume evidence mixes different families
members.description: Failure counts are per family, but session names are indexed only by product. Statistics coverage includes a `family` on each volume check; `over_sessions()` discards it. An `ohlcv-1m` failure can therefore list `tbbo` discrepancies, and vice versa. Preserve family identity and group names by `(product, family)`.

members.title: The provider stack is composed in two places
members.description: `App.tsx:16-24` nests `SymbolTimeframeProvider` and `IndicatorProvider` around the router. `ChartContexts` repeats the same nesting for tests. If App adds or removes a provider, the hook suites still pass and stop reflecting the real tree. CLAUDE.md asks for DRY. Export one composition component and use it in both places.

members.title: File-wide suppression of `react-hooks/refs`
members.description: The rule is turned off for all of `use-chart-provider.ts`. The config comment says it is needed for the `buildChartOperations(runGuarded, series)` call inside the `useMemo` at `use-chart-provider.ts:156-159`. A file-wide `off` also hides any future render-time `.current` read in that file, which is the bug class the rule exists to catch. Narrow the suppression to that line with `// eslint-disable-next-line react-hooks/refs -- <reason>`. I could not run eslint, so the claim that this is a false positive is unverified.

members.title: A whole-file lint suppression is broader than the construct it covers
members.description: `react-hooks/refs` is turned off for all of `use-chart-provider.ts`, which also disables it for any future real violation in that file. The comment attributes the false positive to the `useMemo(() => buildChartOperations(runGuarded, series))` call. If that is accurate, an inline `// eslint-disable-next-line react-hooks/refs` with the reason keeps the rule active for the rest of the file. I could not run eslint to confirm the probe the comment describes.

members.title: The `react-hooks/refs` rule is disabled for the entire hook file
members.description: The suppression applies to every line of `use-chart-provider.ts`, which is where a real render-time `ref.current` read would be written. The rule's purpose is to catch that bug class. The comment justifies the suppression for two `useMemo` calls, at `use-chart-provider.ts:144-154` (the counter) and `:156-159` (the facade). Narrow the suppression to those lines with an inline `eslint-disable-next-line react-hooks/refs` carrying a reason. Then confirm with `pnpm lint` that it is the only trigger. The comment's sentence about the file "~60% over" the guide is also unclear and should be rewritten.

members.title: Blanket `react-hooks/refs` disable for the hook file
members.description: The rule is disabled for all of `use-chart-provider.ts`, so any future real ref-during-render bug in that file goes undetected. The justification is documented and scoped, which is good. `chart-facade.ts` was extracted to get under the 300-line guide, and the hook is still about 366 lines, so the extraction didn't meet that goal. A narrower option is a line-level `eslint-disable-next-line` on the `useMemo` that builds the facade, so the rest of the file stays linted.

members.title: Blanket `except Exception` that does not re-raise
members.description: `_stop_background` catches `Exception` with `# noqa: BLE001`, logs with `logger.exception`, and continues. Project rule (a) requires re-raising after the log, and rule (b) requires a specific exception type. The comment gives a reason, but the rule does not allow a blanket catch in this position. The failure is logged but its outcome is not recorded (see the count finding above). Either record failures and surface them in the dispatch result, or catch the narrowest type the SDK actually raises.

members.title: `get_all_aliases()` re-parses `models.toml` on every call, and the new code calls it on async paths
members.description: `get_all_aliases()` calls `load_builtin_aliases()` and `load_user_aliases()`, which read and parse TOML from disk each time, with no cache. This diff adds a call per resolve (`pipeline/resolver.py:89`, `alias if alias in get_all_aliases()`), which already made about five calls per resolve. It also adds a call per record that has no provider cost (`usage_capture.py:201` → `aliases.py:335` `price_usage`). Both run inside `async def` functions (the dispatch session and one-shot paths and `summary._execute_summary`). The project rule requires synchronous work inside `async def` to take under 1 ms; a parse of this file does not obviously meet that, and I did not measure it. Fix: load the alias table once per process or invalidate on file mtime, or pass the loaded table through the call chain.

members.title: The daemon now depends on the slice-921 repair module
members.description: The steady-state daemon imports `build_truncated_day_index` and `RepairScanTimeout` from `data/gaps/repair_921.py`, a module written as a one-off slice repair. Retiring slice 921 would leave the daemon depending on repair tooling. Move the truncated-day index and its predicate into a shared gaps module that both the daemon and the repair import.

members.title: Production daemon now depends on a one-off repair module
members.description: `minute.py` imports `RepairScanTimeout` and `build_truncated_day_index` from `data.gaps.repair_921`, which is named for a single slice's repair script. The recurring trailing walk now relies on it. Move the truncated-day index into a durable gaps module such as `minute_coverage`, and keep `repair_921` as a consumer of it.

members.title: Production daemon now imports the one-off repair module
members.description:
The daemon depends on `data/gaps/repair_921.py` for `build_truncated_day_index` and `RepairScanTimeout`. A slice-numbered repair module becomes a permanent runtime dependency of the acquisition path. The truncated-day index is now shared logic. Move it into a neutral module such as `minute_coverage` or a `truncated_days` module, and have both the daemon and the repair script import from there.

The daemon also runs this scan on every cycle with a 600s timeout, and a timeout only logs and continues. That is acceptable, but the per-cycle cost is not documented anywhere.

members.title: `build_coverage` has no range guard
members.description: The `end <= start` check exists only in the CLI (`src/manta_trading/cli/commands/tick_store_cmds.py:216-222`). `build_coverage` is the function slice 230's API is meant to serialize (per the `tick_status_build` docstring). With `end <= start`, the session filter `start <= s.session_date < end` matches nothing, so the result has `mismatched: false` and reads as a pass. Fix: validate in `build_coverage` and raise, and keep the CLI's friendly message.

members.title: Run totals omit earlier loop iterations
members.description: The report reads only persisted `action_results`. However, loop execution keeps earlier iterations in `StepResult.prior_rounds`, which `StateManager._append_step()` does not serialize. A reproduced three-round loop costing $0.30 reports $0.10. Persist and include every iteration’s usage, with a regression test covering multi-round execution.

members.title: Run totals omit earlier loop iterations
members.description: The report reads only persisted `action_results`. Loop executors retain earlier iterations in `StepResult.prior_rounds`, but `StateManager._append_step` does not serialize them, and `RunStateRecorder.round_completed` records nothing. A three-call probe persisted only one action. Preserve earlier iterations’ usage and test totals across multiple rounds.

members.title: Run totals omit earlier loop iterations
members.description: The report reads only persisted `action_results`. Earlier loop iterations live in `StepResult.prior_rounds`, which `StateManager._append_step()` does not serialize. A verified two-round example costing $1 and $2 reports only $2. Persist every round’s usage and add a multi-iteration report regression test.
